items.followUp: What is the main cause of goiter, and name one symptom.

rubric.why: Identifies the main cause of goiter.
rubric.description: Cause: insufficient iodine in the diet.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming iodine deficiency as the cause of goiter.

rubric.why: Names a characteristic symptom of goiter.
rubric.description: Symptom: enlargement of the thyroid gland, causing swelling in the neck; it may also cause difficulty swallowing or breathing.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct symptom.

modelAnswer: Goiter is the enlargement of the thyroid gland, usually caused by a deficiency of iodine in the diet.
It produces a visible swelling in the neck and may cause difficulty in swallowing or breathing.

items.followUp: How does wind affect the rate of transpiration?

rubric.why: States the effect of increasing temperature on transpiration.
rubric.description: A rise in temperature generally increases the rate of transpiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that higher temperature increases transpiration.

rubric.why: Explains why higher temperature increases transpiration.
rubric.description: Higher temperature speeds up evaporation of water from leaf surfaces and the diffusion of water vapour out of the leaves.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct explanation involving faster evaporation or diffusion.

modelAnswer: As temperature rises, the rate of transpiration generally increases.
This is because water evaporates more rapidly from leaf surfaces and water vapour diffuses out faster.

items.followUp: Define a population and give one example of a community.

rubric.why: Gives the defining features of a community.
rubric.description: A community consists of populations of different species living and interacting in the same area or habitat.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a definition showing that different populations or species share an area.

rubric.why: Describes a major community and gives or implies a suitable example.
rubric.description: A major community is a large, relatively self-sustaining community, such as a forest.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct description or example of a major community.

rubric.why: Describes a minor community and gives or implies a suitable example.
rubric.description: A minor community is a smaller community that depends on a larger community; examples include organisms living under a log or a small community within a forest.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for describing a minor community and giving a suitable example; award 1 mark for either part alone.

modelAnswer: A community is made up of populations of different species that live and interact in the same area or habitat.
A major community is large and relatively self-sustaining; a forest is an example.
A minor community is smaller and depends on a major community; for example, the organisms living under a log form a minor community within a forest.

items.followUp: Give two differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.

rubric.why: Distinguishes the nuclei of the two cell types.
rubric.description: Prokaryotes lack a membrane-bound nucleus; eukaryotes have a true, membrane-bound nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this correct contrast.

rubric.why: Distinguishes their organelles.
rubric.description: Prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotes possess them.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this correct contrast.

rubric.why: Distinguishes their genetic material.
rubric.description: Prokaryotic DNA is usually circular and not enclosed in a nucleus; eukaryotic DNA is arranged in linear chromosomes in the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct contrast in DNA or chromosomes.

rubric.why: Distinguishes the usual cell sizes.
rubric.description: Prokaryotic cells are generally smaller than eukaryotic cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the correct relative sizes or giving suitable size ranges.

rubric.why: Distinguishes their ribosomes.
rubric.description: Prokaryotes have 70S ribosomes, while eukaryotes have 80S ribosomes in the cytoplasm.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct ribosome contrast.

modelAnswer: Prokaryotic cells have no membrane-bound nucleus; eukaryotic cells have a true, membrane-bound nucleus.
Prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotic cells contain them.
Prokaryotic DNA is usually circular and lies in the nucleoid; eukaryotic DNA is arranged in linear chromosomes inside the nucleus.
Prokaryotic cells are generally smaller, about 1–10 µm, while eukaryotic cells are generally larger, about 10–100 µm.
Prokaryotes have 70S ribosomes; eukaryotes have 80S ribosomes in their cytoplasm.

items.followUp: Write two characteristics of Kingdom Fungi and two of Kingdom Protista.

rubric.why: Gives characteristic features of fungi.
rubric.description: Fungi are eukaryotic organisms; they generally lack chlorophyll and have cell walls made of chitin. Many consist of hyphae forming a mycelium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for at least two accurate fungal features.

rubric.why: Adds a further fungal feature or example.
rubric.description: Fungi include yeasts, moulds and mushrooms; many reproduce by spores.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example or additional characteristic.

rubric.why: Identifies key features or examples of protists.
rubric.description: Protists are eukaryotic and mostly unicellular; examples include Amoeba and Paramecium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for an accurate protist feature or example.

rubric.why: Describes protist diversity or habitat.
rubric.description: Protists are diverse: some, such as algae, make food by photosynthesis, while others, such as protozoans, are heterotrophic; many live in water or moist places.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct contrast, example group, or habitat.

modelAnswer: Kingdom Fungi consists of eukaryotic organisms that lack chlorophyll and absorb nutrients from their surroundings; their cell walls contain chitin.
Many fungi are made of hyphae forming a mycelium and reproduce by spores; examples include moulds, mushrooms and yeast.
Kingdom Protista consists of eukaryotic organisms, most of which are unicellular; examples include Amoeba and Paramecium.
Protists are diverse: algae may make food by photosynthesis, while protozoans are heterotrophic; many live in aquatic or moist environments.

items.followUp: What are the two main types of anaerobic respiration? Give the products of each.

rubric.why: Defines anaerobic respiration.
rubric.description: Anaerobic respiration is the breakdown of glucose to release energy in the absence of oxygen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it occurs without oxygen.

rubric.why: Describes the breakdown and energy release.
rubric.description: Glucose is incompletely broken down, releasing energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing glucose breakdown or energy release.

rubric.why: Identifies alcoholic fermentation and its products.
rubric.description: Alcoholic fermentation, commonly in yeast, produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming this type and its products.

rubric.why: Identifies lactic acid fermentation and its product.
rubric.description: Lactic acid fermentation, occurring in muscle cells during oxygen shortage and in some bacteria, produces lactic acid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming this type and its product.

rubric.why: Provides a correct equation or additional detail about the products or energy yield.
rubric.description: For example, glucose → 2 ethanol + 2 carbon dioxide, or glucose → 2 lactic acid; a small amount of energy is released.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct equation or a correct statement that only a small amount of energy is released.

modelAnswer: Anaerobic respiration is the breakdown of glucose to release energy in the absence of oxygen; glucose is incompletely broken down and yields less energy than aerobic respiration.
Its two main types are alcoholic fermentation and lactic acid fermentation.
In alcoholic fermentation, as in yeast, glucose produces ethanol, carbon dioxide and a small amount of energy: glucose → 2 ethanol + 2 carbon dioxide + energy.
In lactic acid fermentation, as in muscle cells when oxygen is insufficient, glucose produces lactic acid and a small amount of energy: glucose → 2 lactic acid + energy.
Lactic acid fermentation also occurs in some bacteria, such as Lactobacillus.

items.followUp: Name the two sphincters of the stomach and state one function of gastric juice.

rubric.why: Describes the stomach's shape, position or connections.
rubric.description: The stomach is a J-shaped muscular sac in the upper abdomen below the diaphragm, connecting the oesophagus to the duodenum.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct structural description.

rubric.why: Identifies the stomach's sphincters or their positions.
rubric.description: The cardiac sphincter controls entry from the oesophagus and the pyloric sphincter controls exit to the duodenum.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming the two sphincters or correctly describing their positions.

rubric.why: States what the gastric glands or gastric juice contain.
rubric.description: Gastric glands secrete gastric juice, including hydrochloric acid, pepsinogen and mucus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming a correct secretion or its source.

rubric.why: Explains a function of the stomach.
rubric.description: The stomach stores and churns food; its acidic gastric juice helps kill microbes and pepsin begins protein digestion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct function.

modelAnswer: The stomach is a J-shaped, muscular sac in the upper abdomen, below the diaphragm; it connects the oesophagus to the duodenum.
The cardiac sphincter controls the entry of food from the oesophagus, and the pyloric sphincter controls its passage into the duodenum.
Gastric glands in the stomach wall secrete gastric juice containing hydrochloric acid, pepsinogen and protective mucus.
The stomach stores and churns food; its acidic juice helps kill microbes, and pepsin begins the digestion of proteins.

items.followUp: Explain how root hairs absorb water and mineral ions from the soil.

rubric.why: Relates the root-hair structure to absorption.
rubric.description: Root hairs are extensions of epidermal cells; their thin walls and large surface area help them absorb water and mineral ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing root hairs and a structural feature aiding uptake.

rubric.why: Explains water uptake.
rubric.description: Water enters root-hair cells from the soil by osmosis, as the cell sap has a lower water potential than the soil water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming osmosis and giving a correct explanation.

rubric.why: Explains uptake of mineral ions.
rubric.description: Mineral ions may be absorbed by active transport against their concentration gradient, using energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing active uptake of mineral ions.

rubric.why: Describes the route taken by water or ions through the root.
rubric.description: After entering the root, water and ions pass through the cortex and endodermis towards the vascular tissue.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct route through the root tissues.

rubric.why: Connects root uptake to transport through the plant.
rubric.description: Water and mineral salts enter the xylem and are transported upwards through the plant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying xylem as the tissue carrying water and salts upwards.

modelAnswer: Root hairs are extensions of epidermal cells; their thin walls and large surface area provide an effective surface for absorbing water and mineral salts.
Water enters the root-hair cells from the soil by osmosis because the cell sap has a lower water potential than the soil water.
Mineral ions are absorbed by root hairs, often by active transport against their concentration gradient using energy.
Water and ions then move through the cortex and endodermis towards the vascular tissue of the root.
They enter the xylem, which transports water and mineral salts upwards through the plant.
